items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. items.title: Piggybacking to the Frontier
items.content: American data companies like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars worth of data to Chinese AI labs. A chunk of that data comes in the form of reinforcement learning (RL) environments, which labs use to post-train their models to make them excel at specific domains like coding, cyber, finance, law, and bio. Post-training, and especially RL, is one of the most important indicators of the final performance of a model. Whenever a new model within a single generation drops, the advances from the previous release are entirely due to post-training. The difference between Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, or from GPT 5.5 to GPT 5.6, is not due to a new pre-training run. Since they have the same base model, the capability gains come from researchers teaching the model to get better at specific domains. The phenomenon of American companies arming Chinese labs with the data that enables this RL should set off alarms for policymakers and those invested in the U.S.-China AI race: American companies are helping Chinese labs develop better models, and we were able to find at least nine who do so. But the business relationships between data vendors and Chinese labs are more complicated than that single hawkish line, and today, we’re diving into what’s going on. We’ll cover: What it means to sell an RL environment and how it differs from distillation The current ecosystem of China-tied data vendors To what extent American companies are selling RL environments to China Whether this is a problem that needs fixing What RL Does and Doesn’t Look Like Example RL Flows RL environments are essentially simulated worlds in which a model can train to improve its performance at specific tasks or environments. As an example, a model developer may want their model to get better at creating PowerPoint slides with pleasant aesthetics and clear text. To achieve that capability, the model developer may go to a data vendor and ask them to make…

items.title: Why the Cyberpocalypse Might Hit China Harder
items.content: Chang Che is a writer and contributor to the New Yorker . In August, researchers at a California security firm used an OpenAI model to find a software bug in PHP, a programming language that undergird some seventy per cent of the world’s websites, including Wikipedia and WordPress. They alerted PHP’s developers, who quietly began working on a fix. By late October, the fix was ready, but before they could alert the world, the break-in attempts had begun. Days earlier, Amazon detected someone trying to hack into its servers; attacks code began circulating online. Some governments and companies began pulling websites down, rather than risk a security breach. One security firm described the flaws as some of the worst ever found in PHP, “and arguably in software history.” Before AI, the internet might have looked, to a hacker, like a worn-out bug screen. You could discern some holes with a keen eye, and that knowledge was reliably asymmetric—others probably didn’t know about the holes you found. Moreover, tunneling through the holes undetected took months or years of human labor, talent, and money. Now, with AI, the internet looks more like a block of Swiss cheese: the holes are obvious, anyone can, or will, see them, and the time and cost it takes to exploit these software flaws have plunged alarmingly fast . According to Google’s incident response team , the average time it takes for cyber criminals to exploit a new vulnerability is -7 days, meaning hacking attempts are “routinely occurring before a patch is even released.” A China Central Television (CCTV) feature about the PHP vulnerability discovered by cybersecurity firm Calif, with the aid of OpenAI models. Source . Hackers refer to unbeknownst software bugs like PHP as “zero-days” because a defender has had zero days to protect themselves upon its discovery. Once a hacker discovers a zero-day in, say, iOS software, every iPhone user is potentially…

items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.content: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company . In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue . What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode o…

items.title: Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
items.content: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube…   Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. AlphaFold, ESM and BioHub , Chai , Leash , Isomporphic, Boltz , Genesis , Octant, Baker Lab, and many many more. After a lot of initial excitement, Virtual Cell projects have received less attention, due in no small part to questions about the effectiveness of large-scale models in solving even basic Virtual Cell problems. A $1.8B bet The Biohub announcement a few weeks ago got a lot of press for the (really) big numbers: $1.8B of commitments [1] from Biohub, NIH, DOE, Google and Meta. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. View post on X ↗ But why are these organizations doubling down on these big bets now? They have been in the works for years now, what is going on that makes now the moment to push? New measurement capabilities and scale infrastructure, are now coming online that make Biohub’s push likely lead to big impact on science. DOE and NIH are developing lab-in-the-loop automation capabilities at scale. Google is scaling and broadening its connectomics capabilities ( episode coming soon!). Biohub itself has worked with various labs to develop and improve imaging platforms like laser phase plate microscopy, light sheet microscopy and advanced post-processing for regular microscopes that reveal deep phenotypic data. These technologies are quickly maturing, and will likely play a big part in the Biohub ini…
items.summary: As systems biology efforts heat up to map biology at higher resolution, greater breadth and more modalities, Fabian Theis is pushing the frontier from mapping to predicting to controlling biology

However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.content: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the…

items.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. items.title: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?
items.content: Zilan Qian is a research scholar at GovAI researching AI development and regulation in China. On October 21, the People’s Daily published a commentary titled “Turning ‘Gunpowder’ into ‘Fireworks’? Beware the Claim That China’s AI Has Gone Astray” (把”火药”做成”烟花”？警惕”中国AI跑偏论”). The same day, Nanfang Commentary (南方评论), the op-ed column of Southern Daily , asked : “Is Half of China’s Compute Being Spent on Feel-Good Dramas (爽剧)? Don’t Judge AI by Its Tokens.” Three days earlier, Beijing News (新京报) had questioned whether “‘American AI Boosts Productivity While Chinese AI Makes Tittytainment’ Is a False Proposition.” All three state-affiliated outlets were responding to the same viral claim: that 55% of China’s AI tokens were being used for short dramas and video generation. The claim struck a nerve because AI-generated entertainment in China is both everywhere and widely despised. According to China’s broadcasting regulator, more than 90% of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. Yet Chinese media and public figures routinely call them wunao (无脑, braindead), cuzhi lanzao (粗制滥造, shoddily made), and zhili dixia (智力低下, intellectually deficient). 1 Why, in a society that places such a premium on productivity, has an industry devoted to manufacturing seemingly useless pleasure become so enormously popular? And what should we make of the shame attached to it? I argue that both answers lie in Chinese society’s obsession with usefulness, where technologies and people alike are judged by their productive value, so much so that resting can feel…

We also disagree about where the hype is worse: China or America. The conversation is in Mandarin. AI Twitter Recap Gemini 4 Carbon Tops Independent Leaderboards, with Access Limited to Cyber Defenders Launch : Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon two weeks after Argon. It is positioned as state of the art on cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks ( @sundarpichai , @GoogleDeepMind ). Claimed cyber results : 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability finding, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching ( @sundarpichai ). Availability : Carbon first goes to trusted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, with wider developer access promised "as soon as possible" ( @GoogleAI ). Pricing : Phil Schmid quotes $2/$10 per million input/output tokens with an asterisk ( @_philschmid ). Artificial Analysis lists $4/$20 standard pricing with a 50% launch discount that has no end date. Cached input costs $0.20 per million tokens ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Specs : The model has a 1M-token context window and 1M max output. Inputs are text, image, video and speech; output is text ( @ValsAI ). Safety claims (Google) : Successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, and cheating attempts fell to 0.4%. Unsupported claims are down about 2x versus Argon. Overreach fell 26% and under-service fell 29% ( @OfficialLoganK ). Artificial Analysis : Carbon is #1 on Intelligence Index v5 with a score of 59. It leads 4 of the 9 index evals: HLE-Diamond, TB-Science, AA-Omniscience and AutomationBench ( @ArtificialAnlys ). Coding : On the Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59 using Antigravity CLI, versus 62 for Claude Code with Opus 5.5 [max]. It scores 51% on FrontierCode v1.1, versus 56% for Opus. Knowledge work : Carbon reaches 1609 Elo on AA-Briefcase, up 126 points from Argon. It still trails Grok…

items.title: Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots
items.content: The ChinaTalk team is going to CoRL (the Conference on Robot Learning) in Austin! Reply to this email if you’d like to hang out between November 9th and 12th. We’re also doing karaoke on the 11th — RSVP here if you’d like to join! A. Chen writes about people, technologies, and their relationships to power. Her submission, “Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots,” won one of 7 Grand Prizes at the ChinaTalk Essay Contest. We’re thrilled to share this report from the frontlines of China’s robot data collection industry! Where is the center of the universe? For the residents of Beijing, the answer is Wudaokou. The neighborhood houses China’s top universities, research institutions, and labs, drawing talent and funding from every corner of the country. The streets are radiant at night, packed full of bars and clubs that have somehow bounced back after the COVID-19 pandemic. And the number 13 metro line, which rattles overhead every five minutes, is never empty. I came to Wudaokou to understand China’s AI industry — particularly, the hype surrounding humanoid robots, and the methods used to train them. Everyone has seen videos of these robots: eerily tall and lanky, some of them shedding nuts and bolts as they sprint down a track, others backflipping repeatedly on a dance stage. The global market for humanoid robotics, or embodied intelligence, is said to be worth $38 billion by 2035: the latest chapter in the U.S.-China technology race that has dominated international headlines for over a decade. This year, China’s 15 th Five-Year Plan declared embodied intelligence a matter of national priority, then laid a strategy for developing training grounds across the country. Over 150 humanoid robotics companies and 40 state-owned robot data collection centers were reported to be in operation in China by the end of 2025.
